summary: The time of an action stands BEFORE the verb — at the very start of the sentence or right after the subject, never at the end: 我明天去北京 or 明天我去北京 ‘I’m going to Beijing tomorrow’. No preposition is needed: 星期一我工作 ‘on Monday I work’, 晚上我们在家 ‘in the evening we’re at home’. Several time words go from big to small: 明天下午三点 ‘tomorrow at 3 p.m.’, 星期五晚上 ‘Friday evening’. Days are numbered from Monday: 星期一 (1) … 星期六 (6), and Sunday is 星期天 / 星期日; ‘which day?’ is 星期几. A day or date can be the predicate without 是: 今天星期三. Frequency words — 总是 always, 常常 / 经常 often, 有时候 sometimes, 每天 every day — also stand before the verb, and so do 现在 now, 马上 at once, 等一下 / 以后 later. The verb itself never changes: 昨天, 今天 and 明天 alone place the action in time.

blocks.title: Monday is ONE
blocks.text: Chinese counts the weekdays from Monday: 星期一 ‘week-one’ = Monday, 星期二 = Tuesday … 星期六 = Saturday, and Sunday is 星期天 / 星期日. Hebrew יוֹם שֵׁנִי ‘second day’ and Arabic الاثنين ‘the second’ count from Sunday and mean Monday — in Chinese the ‘second’ day, 星期二, is Tuesday.

blocks.title: Never at the end
blocks.text: *我去北京明天, with the time at the end, is wrong. Chinese: 我明天去北京. The time frames the action, so it comes first.

items.title: 每天 / 天天 — every day
points: 我每天跑步。 I run every day.
每 + 天 / 个 + noun: 每个星期一

items.title: 有时候 — sometimes
points: 有时候 … 有时候 … ‘sometimes … sometimes …’

blocks.title: No tense: the time word does the work
blocks.text: 昨天我在家 ‘yesterday I was at home’, 今天我在家 ‘today I’m at home’, 明天我在家 ‘tomorrow I’ll be at home’ — 在 never changes. (For a completed action Chinese adds 了 — see the aspect page.)

blocks.title: Asking about time
blocks.text: 今天星期几？ ‘what day is it?’ — 星期四。 · 你什么时候去？ — 明天下午。 · 你常常来吗？ The question word stands where the answer stands.

askYourself: Does my sentence say when? → put the time word before the verb — at the start or after the subject.
Several time words? → big to small: day → part of the day → hour (明天下午三点).
Time and place? → time first, then 在 + place, then the verb (晚上我们在家吃饭).
Which day? → 星期 + 1–6, Sunday 星期天 / 星期日; ask 星期几.
Did I add ‘on / in / at’? → remove it: 星期一我工作.
How often? → 总是 / 常常 / 经常 / 有时候 / 每天 before the verb (after the subject).
Did I put the time at the end? → move it before the verb.

traps: *我去北京明天 → 我明天去北京.
*在星期一我工作 (in speech) → 星期一我工作.
星期一 is Monday and 星期二 Tuesday — don’t carry over a week that is counted from Sunday.
*星期七 → 星期天 / 星期日.
*我们在家晚上吃饭 → 晚上我们在家吃饭 (time before place).
*三个天 → 三天 (天 counts by itself).
早上好 is the greeting; ‘in the morning’ is just 早上: 我早上喝茶.

quiz.why: Time before the verb, never at the end.
几 takes the place of the day’s number.
No preposition; the day stands first (or after 我).
Big to small: day, part of the day, hour.
Frequency words stand before the verb.

quiz.q: ‘In the evening we eat at home.’
quiz.why: Time first, then the place, then the verb.

notes.text: Greek Δευτέρα ‘second’ is Monday and Τρίτη ‘third’ Tuesday, counted from Sunday; Chinese 星期一 is Monday and 星期二 Tuesday. Greek, too, needs no preposition with days (τη Δευτέρα), but its time words can go anywhere; Chinese ones go before the verb.
Russian вторник ‘second’ = Tuesday = 星期二 and четверг ‘fourth’ = Thursday = 星期四 — the same count from Monday. в понедельник needs в; Chinese 星期一 needs nothing and stands before the verb.
Spanish days are named after planets and gods (lunes, martes); Chinese ones are numbered from Monday (星期一, 星期二). el lunes needs the article; Chinese 星期一 needs nothing and stands before the verb.
English names the days (Monday, Tuesday), needs ‘on’ / ‘in’, and puts the time at the end (I work on Monday); Chinese numbers the days and puts the time first, with no preposition: 星期一我工作.
French lundi, mardi are planetary names; Chinese days are numbered: 星期一, 星期二. le lundi for a habit has no Chinese equivalent — 星期一 alone, before the verb.
German Montag, Dienstag are names, though Mittwoch ‘mid-week’ counts; Chinese numbers them all: 星期一, 星期三. am Montag ~ 星期一, with no word for ‘on’, and the time always before the verb.
Hindi सोमवार ‘moon-day’, मंगलवार ‘Mars-day’ are planetary names; Chinese days are numbers. Hindi also puts time words before the verb (मैं कल जाऊँगा ‘I’ll go tomorrow’), as Chinese does.
Persian numbers the days from Saturday: doshanbe ‘two-shanbe’ is Monday, seshanbe Tuesday; Chinese numbers from Monday: 星期一 Monday, 星期二 Tuesday. The same number names a different day.
Marathi सोमवार, मंगळवार are planetary names; Chinese days are numbers from Monday. Marathi, like Chinese, puts the time before the verb (मी उद्या जाईन ‘I’ll go tomorrow’).
Arabic al-ithnayn ‘the second’ is Monday and al-thulāthāʾ ‘the third’ Tuesday, counted from Sunday; Chinese 星期二 ‘week-two’ is Tuesday.
Hebrew yom sheni ‘second day’ is Monday, counted from Sunday; Chinese 星期二 is Tuesday — the same number, the next day.
Turkish days have names (Pazartesi, Salı); Chinese ones are numbered from Monday. Turkish puts the time before the verb (yarın gidiyorum), as Chinese does (我明天去), with no preposition.
Japanese 月曜日 ‘moon day’ uses planetary names, so the characters do not match: Monday is 星期一. Months do match (一月, 二月), and Japanese also puts the time before the verb.
Korean 월요일 ‘moon day’ uses planetary names; Chinese numbers the days: 星期一. Korean, like Chinese, puts time words before the verb (내일 가요 ~ 明天去).
Finnish maanantai, tiistai are names, and maanantaina takes a case ending; Chinese numbers the days from Monday, and 星期一 needs nothing.
Hungarian hétfő ‘week head’ = Monday and szerda ‘middle’ = Wednesday; Chinese simply counts: 星期一, 星期三. hétfőn takes a case ending; Chinese 星期一 needs nothing.
Swahili numbers its days from Saturday (Jumamosi ‘day one’ = Saturday, Jumatatu ‘day three’ = Monday); Chinese numbers from Monday (星期一). Same idea, different start — the numbers do not match.
Luganda counts several weekdays too, and Lwakubiri ‘the second’ is Tuesday — like 星期二. Chinese numbers all of them from Monday: 星期一 … 星期六, and Sunday is 星期天.
Vietnamese thứ hai ‘second’ is Monday and thứ ba Tuesday; Chinese 星期二 is Tuesday. Vietnamese time words can go at the start or the end; Chinese ones go before the verb.
Inuktitut marks time with suffixes inside the verb word; Chinese marks it only with separate time words before the verb (明天, 星期一), and the verb never changes.

seeAlso.note: German uses am (am Montag, am Abend) and in der Nacht but nothing with heute / morgen / gestern; it often opens with the time and keeps the verb second (Morgen fahre ich nach Peking). Chinese needs no preposition and puts the verb after the time: 明天我去北京.

Arabic days count from Sunday (الأحد ‘the first’, الاثنين ‘the second’ = Monday), so الاثنين = 星期一; ‘on Monday’ is يَوْمَ الِاثْنَيْنِ, an accusative of time without a preposition — like Chinese, but with a case ending.

Hebrew days are numbered from Sunday (יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן … יוֹם שִׁשִּׁי, then שַׁבָּת), so יוֹם שֵׁנִי ‘the second day’ = 星期一 ‘week-one’; ‘on Monday’ is בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי with בְּ־, where Chinese uses nothing.
Time words say WHEN; 了 / 过 / 在 say whether the action is done, experienced or going on.
